UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,
Defendants.

EXHIBIT A

PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SUPPLEMENTAL MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF
ECF NO. 15 ADDRESSING NCMEC’S RENEWED TRUTH
AND LACK-OF-ACCESS ARGUMENTS

This memorandum supplements the briefing on Plaintiff’s pending Rule 26(d)(1) motion.
ECF No. 15. It addresses the opposition Defendants Katie Hall and NCMEC filed on September
18, 2026. ECF No. 74. It changes nothing about the discovery requested.

I. NCMEC Again Relies on Plaintiff’s Lack of Access to Support Dismissal.

ECF No. 74 states that Plaintiff “cannot plausibly assert falsity, because he does not have
access to those reports.” ECF No. 74 at 5. ECF No. 74 continues: “[n]Jo allegations Plaintiff can
make can change that fact.” Id. The word “fact” refers to Plaintiff’s lack of access. NCMEC
invokes the reports’ asserted contents to defeat the claims. NCMEC invokes Plaintiff’s inability to

inspect the reports to defeat any challenge. One informational gap does both jobs.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 2 of 7 PagelD#
785

The categorical position is wrong. Allegations pled on information and belief “are not
categorically insufficient to state a claim for relief where the proof supporting the allegation is
within the sole possession and control of the defendant or where the belief is based on sufficient
factual material that makes the inference of culpability plausible.” Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC,
No. 24-1822, slip op. at 34-35 (4th Cir. Feb. 11, 2026) (quoting Ahern Rentals, Inc. v.
EquipmentShare.com, Inc., 59 F.4th 948, 954 (8th Cir. 2023)). Lowy is a published decision. Lowy
reversed a dismissal entered in this Division on the papers.

Lowy does not itself authorize discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference. Lowy forecloses
the categorical premise: that lack of access defeats Plaintiff’s allegations as a class. ECF No. 74
asks the Court to adopt that premise. NCMEC opposes the three answers directed to it. ECF No. 15
requests those answers. The premise should be tested, not assumed.

Il. NCMEC’s “Any” Formulation Permits Materially Different Source Facts.

ECF No. 74 describes the statements at issue as concerning CyberTipline reports received
“for any of the three identifiers in Plaintiff’s subpoena to NCMEC.” ECF No. 74 at 5. That sentence
is NCMEC’s litigation characterization. It is not the text of the April 22, 2026 letters.

First, “any” identifies no particular matching term. A report satisfies the formulation if it
matched one identifier out of three.

Second, the formulation is consistent with the absence of “Marvelle J. Ballentine” from
both reports as originally received. A report matching only “Jay Ballentine,” or only the email
address, satisfies the formulation.

Third, NCMEC’s August 12 memorandum supplied a different alternative: “a person with
the same name.” ECF No. 11 at 9. A report concerning a different person with the same name

would not concern Plaintiff.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 3 of 7 PagelD#
786

Fourth, the three interrogatories address the facts both formulations leave unspecified. Each
asks whether either report, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified
one named identifier. ECF No. 15-1 at 1-2.

The two open questions are distinct. The absence of “Marvelle J. Ballentine” from a report
would not, by itself, establish that the report did not concern Plaintiff through his alias or his email
address. The name question concerns the reports’ original identifying information. The different-
person question concerns personal identity. Each answer narrows one of them. Neither formulation
NCMEC has offered resolves either one. NCMEC defends a disjunction. The interrogatories ask
which branch or branches of it are true.

II. _Plaintiff’s Declaration Supplies a Concrete Basis for the Source Question.

Plaintiff has sworn to his account-naming history. Plaintiff did not use “Marvelle J.
Ballentine” to create, identify, or operate any Meta account. Plaintiff used “Jay Ballentine.”
Plaintiff supplied his full legal name in the April 9, 2026 materials because it is his legal name. ECF
No. 31 44 3-8.

Those facts distinguish two sources. One is information Plaintiff supplied through litigation
materials. The other is identifying information contained in the reports when NCMEC originally
received them. Interrogatory No. 1 tests that distinction. It excludes the April 9 materials, court
filings, public sources, and information obtained or added after original receipt. ECF No. 15-1 at 1.

The request is not open-ended. It names two identified reports, three identifiers, one fixed
point in time, and stated exclusions. It permits three answers. It seeks no explanation and no report
content.

The declaration has limits, and the request respects them. The declaration establishes

Plaintiff’s own account practices. It does not identify the submitting provider or every possible

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 4 of 7 PagelD#
787

source of a report’s contents. The interrogatories put the source question to the entity that holds the
reports.

IV. NCMEC Identifies the Reports as Material Evidence; Plaintiff Seeks Less than

Production.

ECF No. 74 states that if Plaintiff had access to the reports, they “presumably would be
exhibits to the pleading, or provided under seal to the Court for review.” ECF No. 74 at 5. That
sentence treats the reports as the evidence bearing on this dispute. That sentence identifies a sealed-
review path. NCMEC holds the reports. No defendant in either action has filed a CyberTipline
report, openly or under seal.

The sentence also demands proof at the pleading stage. Plaintiffs are not required “to prove
[their] case in the complaint,” and the requirement of factual detail is “tempered by the recognition
that a plaintiff may only have so much information at [her] disposal at the outset.” Lowy, slip op. at
22 (quoting Robertson v. Sea Pines Real Est. Cos., 679 F.3d 278, 291 (4th Cir. 2012)). A court may
consider the April 22 letters for their language without accepting their assertions as true. Goines v.
Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d 159, 167-69 (4th Cir. 2016). Pleading the letters does not make
the letters proof of their own truth.

The consequences NCMEC seeks sharpen the timing. NCMEC requests dismissal with
prejudice. ECF No. 11 at 17, NCMEC opposes amendment as futile and asks that leave await
rulings on the motions to dismiss. ECF No. 74 at 5—7. Both requests rest on what the reports are
said to establish. Plaintiff has asked three questions about those reports. NCMEC opposes the

answe!s.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 5 of 7 PagelD#
788

The scope of this argument is narrow. Plaintiff draws no waiver from NCMEC’s sealed-
review reference. Plaintiff requests no adverse inference from nonproduction. This motion requests
neither the reports nor a sealing procedure. It requests three answers.

V. Three Sworn Answers Test NCMEC’s Chosen Premise with Defined Burden.

The pending interrogatories read in full:

INTERROGATORY NO. 1: Excluding information supplied by Plaintiff in the

April 9, 2026 materials, court filings, public sources, and information obtained or

added after original receipt by NCMEC, did either of the two CyberTipline reports

referenced in NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters, as originally received by NCMEC,
contain or otherwise identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”?

INTERROGATORY NO. 2: Subject to the same exclusions, did either report, as
originally received by NCMEC, contain or otherwise identify “Jay Ballentine”?

INTERROGATORY NO. 3: Subject to the same exclusions, did either report, as
originally received by NCMEC, contain’ or _ otherwise _ identify
jaychizza@icloud.com?

ECF No. 15-1 at 1-2. NCMEC shall answer each interrogatory only “Yes,” “No,” or
“Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry.” Id. at 1. The interrogatories seek no explanation
and no report content. Id. Each asks about either report. None requires a report-by-report mapping.
None asks why a match occurred.

Rule 26(d)(1) permits discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference by court order.
Relevance, timing, access, and burden point the same way. NCMEC selected the two reports and
the three identifiers as the factual basis of its defense. NCMEC holds the reports. NCMEC seeks

claim-terminating relief now. The burden is three sworn one-sentence answers under Rule 33,

within the response period requested in ECF No. 15 or the period the Court directs.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 78-1 Filed 09/18/26 Page 6 of 7 PagelD#
789

The answers have defined value and defined limits. Each answer fixes or narrows one
original-source fact. No answer determines ownership of an alias, defamatory meaning, or liability.
Plaintiff does not contend that every ground in the motions to dismiss requires discovery. Plaintiff
requests resolution of the source question before any relief that depends on accepting NCMEC’s
account of what the reports establish.

CONCLUSION

The Court should grant ECF No. 15 on its existing terms and consider ECF No. 74 as
further support for the present need for the three answers. NCMEC’s “any” formulation leaves the

identifying facts unspecified. ECF No. 15 asks for those facts, under oath, without requesting the

reports.

Date: September 18, 2026 Respectfully submitted,
